messages.subject: Spatial line transect models
messages.body_plain:
I'm in the process of extrapolating density estimates based on model cova=
riates following this basic procedure:
1) do transect-based surveys using relatively short and numerous transect=
s
2) estimate densities in different habitat types
3) extrapolate densities to the transect level by dividing the observed c=
ount of organisms along a transect divided by (2 * Effective Strip Width =
* length of transect)
4) use GLM/GAM modeling to model transect-level density estimates as a fu=
nction of habitat covariates
5) extrapolate model across a geographic area

I have a question relating to steps 3 & 4.  Basically, wouldn't one expec=
t zero-inflation in step 3 because you're effectively multiplying an obse=
rved density by a scaling factor, but multiplying an observed density of =
0 times a scaling factor doesn't alter the observed density to account fo=
r detectability.  I don't see anything in Advanced Distance sampling (par=
ticularly section 4.3.2) regarding this.  If it's already been addressed =
somewhere, I'd love to be pointed in the right direction!  I'm using zero=
-inflated modeling to attempt to account for this, and I would like to kn=
ow if my overall conceptualization of the issue is valid (see below for m=
ore details on my conceptualization).=20

Thanks!
Philip Shirk

If my short explanation didn't make sense, here's a more detailed attempt=
 to explain it:

In order to estimate detectability, distance-based density estimation use=
s the combined data from all transects.  (Individual transects are needed=
 only to estimate variation in the estimate.)  Conceptually, the observed=
 density is always below the true density because one can miss an organis=
m that is actually present, but one cannot see an organism that is not th=
ere (this can be ensured by excluding any uncertain =E2=80=9Csightings=E2=
=80=9D from the analysis).  The estimate of detectability is then used as=
 a scaling factor to adjust observed densities to account for detectabili=
ty.  Similarly, density can be extrapolated down to the individual transe=
ct using the effective transect width as a scaling factor for the observe=
d densities.  This is useful when organisms were observed along a transec=
t.  However, when no organisms were observed along a transect, multiplyin=
g a scaling factor times zero does not alter the estimate.  In the case w=
here no organisms were observed because there were no organisms to observ=
e, the final estimate of zero density is still correct.  When no organism=
s are observed because of poor detection, the scaling factor fails to acc=
ount for this because it is being multiplied times zero.  As a result, tr=
ansect-level density estimates will be zero-inflated, despite an accurate=
 regional density estimate.  As we expect excess zeros, zero-inflated mod=
els may be most useful for modeling transect-level density estimates.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I plan to use Distance to design line surveys to determine the key areas =
of habitat of a community of common dolphins that we regularly find close=
 to shore in Port Phillip. I have managed to create two shapefiles of the=
 areas I intend to cover during my vessel surveys in ESRI=E2=80=99s ArcMa=
p from a shapefile of Port Phillip.=20=20

I have imported the survey area shapefiles into Distance as described for=
 the Mexico project by copying the files and renaming them in the datafol=
der.  As suggested, I have also created an additional field =E2=80=98Link=
ID=E2=80=99 (long integer) in ArcCatalog. Once in Distance I can open and=
 view each of the shapefiles as a correctly projected map in the map tab.=
  The shapefiles use GDA 94 and transverse mercatore coordinates as per t=
he original map and are the setting used as the default in Distance.=20=20=

My problem arises when working with the file in the datatab.  If I open t=
he shape properties dialog by double clicking the blank shape field type =
there are no x and y coordinates listed and no vertices although the file=
 is recognised as a polygon.  Without the x y coordinates I am unable to =
produce coverage girds and consequently cannot produce my desired line tr=
ansects.  I am using ArcView and do not have access to ArcInfo to be able=
 to be able to convert my shapefile to vertices that can be cut and paste=
 directly into the shape properties dialog window. Is there a way to obta=
in the x and y coordinates?=20

Thank you in advance.

Sue Mason
PhD student=20
Curtin University

messages.subject: Model Choice
messages.body_plain:
I have two competing detection functions in estimating density estimates
from line transect data with same truncation level and class intervals.
While both of them provide very similar AIC values, chi-sqaure value is
significant for one of the models. The model with non-significant
chi-square value is Negative exponential plus simple polynomial. However,
this gives unacceptably high density estimates. The model with significant
chi-square value (ie. Halfnormal with Simple Polynomial) gives reasonable
estimate. Should I go strictly with model with lowest AIC and
non-significant chi-sqaure value?. Any one can advice me.

Sivaram

--

messages.subject: Re: Model Choice
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sivaram, list,

This is a recurrent question posted to the list. The fundamental point=20
is to understand why is it that the HN model produces a significant GOF=20
statistic. I would say, based on what you are describing, that you have=20
many small distances (maybe even too many 0 distances) that lead to a=20
spiked detection function. What is funny is that in such cases quite=20
often the AIC favours strongly the NE, which does not seem to be the=20
case for your data.

I would say that blindly using AIC or GOF measures is never the best=20
approach. One needs to understand the data, and model accordingly. If=20
say you have a measurement error problem, with too many distances=20
recorded as 0, a model like the HN will likely provide you better=20
density estimates than the more than likely overestimation given the NE=20
is used.

Of course, even better for next time, would be to identify what might be=20
the cause of the problem and solve it by changing survey/field methods.

All the best,

Tiago
